name: iat
desc: Converts many CD-ROM image formats to ISO9660
why: Converts obscure CD-ROM image formats into ISO9660, a small but real dive into disc layouts.

brief.what_it_is: iat (Iso9660 Analyzer Tool) is a small C console program, licensed GPLv2, for Linux and Windows. Per its SourceForge summary, it has an engine that detects many structures of CD-ROM image files. The Homebrew description says it converts many CD-ROM image formats to ISO9660, but the SourceForge page itself describes detection and analysis, and I saw no explicit conversion statement there. Input is an image file in one of those formats; the output is described as an ISO9660 image.
brief.why_it_exists: The SourceForge summary gives no stated motivation beyond describing the tool as an analyzer for disc image structures. The scout note frames it as a way to handle obscure CD-ROM image formats by converting them to ISO9660.
brief.install_notes: No install steps were visible on the SourceForge pages. The files listing offers source tarballs (iat-0.1.7.tar.gz, .tar.bz2, .tar.lzma, .zip, .shar.gz) and a Windows zip (iat-0.1.7.win32.zip). The Homebrew formula is the simplest route on macOS or Linux. Build steps and any usage instructions were not found.
brief.standout: It is an old, small, single-purpose C tool that tries to recognise many odd disc image layouts and normalise them to ISO9660. That makes it a compact way to read how those formats are laid out.
brief.status: Quiet. The SourceForge page labels it Status: Alpha and shows Last Update 2014-06-09, but the newest downloadable release is iat-0.1.7, dated 2009-08-25, and the source file iat.c is dated 2007-02-08. No README, changelog, or recent commits were visible. The project was registered 2006-06-01.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a SourceForge page with no README, so the information is thin. The Alpha label, the age of the releases, and the lack of documentation all point to limited maintenance. The page only lists Linux and Windows. The sourceforge.net project also appears in a SourceForge recommendation note that says the site is no longer maintained for many projects, though that note refers to DUMA, not iat. The license is GPLv2. Which input formats are supported was not listed on the page.
